title: Enya
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Cassava flour, often cut with millet or sorghum, mingled into boiling water until it leaves the stick clean — West Nile's staple, and the thing every Lugbara sauce is eaten with.
longDesc: Enya, or enyasa, is the Lugbara staple: cassava flour, often mixed with millet or sorghum, mingled into a stiff mass and served with soups. It is the same class of dish as kalo and atapa in Ateso, as fufu further west in Africa, and as posho or ugali — the Lugbara sources give exactly those equivalents. Everything in the Lugbara kitchen is eaten with it, which is why it closes out that community's entries here rather than opening them.
ingredients: Millet or sorghum flour, to mix in
// No quantities are documented for enya. The karo ratio, 3 litres of water to a kilo of flour, is the nearest documented guide
steps: Bring the water to the boil.
Add the flour gradually while stirring continuously, to prevent air pockets.
Work it until the water has reduced, then add more hot water — never cold, which sets the flour stiff.
Keep mingling until the mixture no longer sticks to the stirring stick.
Turn it out, shape it, cover it and rest it briefly.
Serve with a soup or sauce.
chefTips: No longer sticking to the stick. That is the cue, shared with karo, atapa and posho.
Hot water for any addition after the first. Cold water sets the flour stiff and ends the batch.
Cassava flour alone is workable in a way millet alone is not, which is why the mixes go the other way here — millet or sorghum added to a cassava base rather than cassava added to a millet base.

Be clear about the sourcing: the Lugbara source describes enya as cassava flour often mixed with millet or sorghum and served with soups, and gives no method at all. The mingling technique in the steps comes from karo, UGA091, which is the same class of dish and is documented with quantities. That is a cross-reference, not an attestation.
The documented equivalents are worth knowing because the source gives them: kalo and atap or atapa in Ateso, fufu, and posho or ugali. It is the same idea across a continent.
It is served with soups, and in the Lugbara kitchen that means osubi and the other greens, kila kila, operete, nzikinziki and the ant dishes.
Rice, yams, potatoes and matooke are also eaten in West Nile — enya is the staple, not the only starch.
commonMistakes: Adding the flour all at once.
Stopping before it leaves the stick clean.
Using a weak spoon — this needs a real mingling stick.
sources: The dish is documented in the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine as the staple: cassava flour, enya or enyasa, often mixed with millet or sorghum and served with soups, with the equivalents given as kalo and atap or atapa in Ateso, fufu, and posho or ugali. That article also records that rice, yams, potatoes and matooke are eaten in West Nile. It gives no method and no quantities.

The mingling method in the steps is taken from the Ankole karo chapter of the Wikibooks project 'Mujje Tulye from Uganda', which documents the same class of dish with quantities — three litres of water to a kilo of flour, gradual flour addition to prevent air pockets, hot water only for later additions, and the no-longer-adheres-to-the-utensil cue. That is a cross-reference from a related dish and is labelled as such rather than presented as an attestation for enya.
The Lugbara cuisine article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material, so its detail is treated as a lead rather than as established fact.
storage: Best fresh. It firms considerably as it cools.
reheating: Steam briefly, or eat it cold.
healthBenefits: Cassava flour is naturally gluten-free and high in resistant starch.
Millet or sorghum in the mix adds iron, calcium and B vitamins.
Flour and water only, with no fat at all.
Very filling and slow to release its energy.
culturalNote: Every African region has its stiff starch and each one insists its own is different, which is both true and beside the point — the technique is identical from Accra to Arua and the flour is whatever grows. That the Lugbara source lists fufu and ugali as equivalents without embarrassment is a refreshingly unterritorial way to describe your own staple.
